title: Multi-Turn Context Drift and the 'Lost in the Middle' Effect
content: Long conversations and long contexts don't just cost more -- they can measurably degrade an agent's behavior, a phenomenon this course covers under two related ideas. Context drift describes how, over many turns, a conversation can accumulate noise, tangents, and even outright contradictions (a user changes their mind, or an earlier assumption turns out to be wrong), and if the agent keeps weighing everything in the accumulated history equally, its behavior can drift away from the current, correct state of the task. The 'lost in the middle' effect describes a documented tendency for models to attend more reliably to information near the beginning and end of a long context than to content buried in the middle, meaning a critical instruction or fact placed in the middle of a very long prompt can be effectively under-weighted even though it's technically present. You'll learn practical mitigations for both: periodically re-injecting key instructions or the current, corrected state near the end of the context (closer to where the model is about to generate) rather than relying on something stated many turns ago, and actively pruning or correcting outdated information from history instead of letting contradictions accumulate silently.

quiz.question: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect?
options: Models perform equally well regardless of where information sits in a long context
A documented tendency for models to attend less reliably to information placed in the middle of a long context compared to the beginning or end
A bug that only affects very short prompts
An effect that only applies to system prompts, never user content

quiz.question: Why can 'context drift' cause an agent to behave incorrectly even though the correct information was stated earlier in the conversation?
options: The correct information is always weighted most heavily automatically
If contradictions or outdated assumptions accumulate and are weighed equally with corrected information, the agent's behavior can drift away from the current correct state
Context drift is not a real phenomenon
Longer conversations always improve accuracy over time

quiz.question: What is a practical mitigation for the 'lost in the middle' effect on a critical instruction?
options: Removing the instruction from the prompt entirely
Re-injecting the key instruction closer to the end of the context, nearer to where the model is about to generate
Always placing critical instructions in the exact middle of the prompt
Increasing temperature to compensate

title: Context Engineering Certification Assessment
content: This capstone validates practical context engineering judgment: architecting what goes into a model's context, budgeting a limited context window across competing needs, managing memory across sessions, and recognizing degradation from context drift or the 'lost in the middle' effect. Before attempting it you should be comfortable explaining the difference between prompt engineering and context engineering, how to allocate context budget across system instructions, retrieved knowledge, and history, and why compression and memory management both carry a real risk of losing or misapplying information. The questions are scenario-driven: given a long-running agent whose behavior degrades over a lengthy conversation, can you diagnose whether the cause is context drift, budget exhaustion, or a 'lost in the middle' placement issue, and propose the right fix? Passing signals you could debug a real context-management problem in production, not just define the terms.

quiz.question: An agent's answers become inconsistent and occasionally contradict earlier correct statements as a conversation grows very long. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model has run out of storage space
Context drift, where accumulated noise and contradictions in history are being weighed alongside corrected information
This is always caused by a hardware failure
Long conversations never affect agent behavior

quiz.question: A critical instruction placed in the middle of a very long system prompt is being followed inconsistently. What is a likely explanation and fix?
options: The instruction should be removed since it's clearly wrong
The 'lost in the middle' effect; moving or re-injecting the instruction closer to the end of the context can help
This is unrelated to context placement and can't be fixed
Adding more unrelated content will resolve it

quiz.question: A system's cost and latency are climbing over a long session while quality also degrades. Where should you look first?
options: The underlying model must be replaced immediately
Context budgeting: unbounded history or excessive retrieved content may be crowding out relevant, current information
This can only be a network issue
Nothing can be done once a session grows long

quiz.question: What is this capstone primarily assessing?
options: Memorization of context engineering terminology
Practical judgment in diagnosing and fixing real context-management problems in a running system
Speed of prompt writing
Knowledge of an unrelated domain

title: How Token Pricing Works
content: Most LLM providers price API usage per token, typically quoted as a rate per one million tokens, and understanding this billing unit is the foundation for every cost decision that follows. This course covers the basic calculation: total cost for a request equals input tokens processed times the input rate, plus output tokens generated times the output rate, and these two rates are usually different from each other. You'll walk through a concrete example: if a provider charges $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, a request with a 2,000-token prompt and a 500-token response costs roughly (2,000 / 1,000,000 x $3) + (500 / 1,000,000 x $15) -- about $0.006 for input plus $0.0075 for output, around $0.0135 total, which sounds trivial per call but adds up quickly at scale: a feature serving 100,000 requests a day at that rate is already over $1,300 a day. You'll learn why teams need to estimate token counts before shipping a feature, not just track spend after the fact, since a seemingly small per-request cost can become a large recurring expense once multiplied by real usage volume.

sections.heading: Tokens as the Billing Unit -- Why Not Characters or Words?
sections.body: LLM providers don't bill by the character or the word -- they bill by the token, the actual unit the model's tokenizer breaks text into. A tokenizer like OpenAI's tiktoken (BPE-based) or Anthropic's equivalent splits text into subword pieces: common English words often map to a single token, rarer words split into two or three, and as a rough rule of thumb one token averages about 4 characters or roughly 0.75 words. This matters practically -- "tokenization" itself might be two tokens, while "the" is one. Non-English text, code, and unusual formatting (JSON with lots of punctuation, for example) tend to tokenize less efficiently, sometimes 1.5-2x more tokens per character than plain English prose. Providers quote rates per one million tokens (e.g., "$3 / 1M input tokens") precisely because token count, not character count, is what determines the compute the model actually does -- and therefore what the provider charges you for.

sections.heading: The Cost Formula: Input Rate Plus Output Rate
sections.body: Every request's cost breaks into exactly two terms: (input tokens x input rate) + (output tokens x output rate). These are tracked and billed separately because a single API call consumes both -- the tokens you send in the prompt and the tokens the model generates in response -- and providers meter them independently. Take a provider charging $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens: a request with a 2,000-token prompt and a 500-token response costs (2,000 / 1,000,000 x $3) = $0.006 for input, plus (500 / 1,000,000 x $15) = $0.0075 for output, for a total of $0.0135. Note the output half is more than half the total cost despite being a quarter of the token count -- that asymmetry in rate, not just volume, is why teams model the two terms separately rather than treating "tokens" as one undifferentiated cost bucket.

sections.heading: Why Output Tokens Cost More Than Input Tokens
sections.body: Input and output rates differ -- often by 3x to 5x, sometimes more -- because the two operations aren't computationally equivalent. Processing input tokens is largely parallelizable: the model can ingest and encode the entire prompt in one forward pass, and providers can batch many requests' prompts together efficiently, plus cache repeated prefixes (system prompts, few-shot examples) to avoid recomputing them. Generating output tokens is autoregressive -- the model produces one token, feeds it back in, produces the next, one at a time, sequentially, which is far harder to parallelize and batch across requests. That sequential dependency means generation consumes more GPU time per token than encoding does. Providers pass that cost difference straight through: input tokens are priced as "reading" cost, output tokens as "writing" cost, and the higher output rate is a direct reflection of the heavier, less parallelizable compute generation requires.

sections.heading: From Per-Call Pennies to Per-Day Line Items
sections.body: A $0.0135 request looks negligible in isolation -- it's the kind of number that's easy to wave away in a design review. But cost per call is only half the picture; the other half is call volume, and production features rarely stay small. At 100,000 requests a day, that same $0.0135 becomes $1,350 a day, or roughly $40,000 a month, and $480,000+ annualized -- all from a single feature at a single usage tier, before any traffic growth. The arithmetic is linear and unforgiving: doubling daily active users doubles the bill, adding a second LLM call per request (a re-ranking step, a verification pass) roughly doubles it again. Costs that look trivial at prototype scale (a few dozen test calls) and costs that look alarming at production scale (hundreds of thousands of calls) are the exact same per-token rate -- only the multiplier changed.

sections.heading: Estimating Before You Ship, Not Just Tracking After
sections.body: Because the per-request cost multiplies directly into a recurring expense, the right time to compute it is during design, not after the invoice arrives. Before shipping, estimate: average prompt length in tokens (system prompt + retrieved context + user input, if any), expected output length, and projected daily call volume -- then run the same formula used for a single request across that volume to get a daily and monthly figure. This catches problems a post-hoc spend dashboard catches too late: a verbose system prompt repeated on every call, an output length that balloons past what the feature needs, or a call pattern (looping, retries, chained sub-calls) that silently multiplies token usage per user action. Estimating ahead turns a possible end-of-month surprise into a known, budgeted number, and gives you the chance to redesign -- shorter prompts, capped output length, caching -- before the cost is already locked in at scale.

quiz.question: What are the two main components of the cost formula for a single LLM API request?
options: Only the number of input tokens matters
Input tokens times the input rate, plus output tokens times the output rate
A flat fee regardless of token count
Cost is based solely on latency, not tokens

quiz.question: Why do input and output tokens typically have different prices?
options: They are always priced identically
Providers set separate rates, and output tokens are usually priced higher reflecting the cost of generation
Input tokens are never billed at all
Pricing is randomly assigned per request

quiz.question: Why is it important to estimate token costs before shipping a feature, not just track spend afterward?
options: Pre-launch estimation is unnecessary since costs are always negligible
A small per-request cost can become a large recurring expense once multiplied by real usage volume, and estimating ahead avoids surprises
Token costs cannot be estimated in advance under any circumstances
Only output tokens ever need to be considered

title: Input vs. Output Token Costs: Why They Differ
content: Across most providers, output tokens cost noticeably more per token than input tokens, often several times as much, and this course explains why that asymmetry exists and what it implies for how you design a system. Processing input tokens (the 'prefill' stage) can largely happen in parallel -- the model can process the entire prompt's tokens together in one pass. Generating output tokens happens autoregressively, one token at a time, where each new token depends on all the previous ones, making generation inherently more sequential and computationally expensive per token. You'll learn the practical design implication: a verbose system that generates long explanations, extensive reasoning traces, or repeats large amounts of input back in its output pays a disproportionate cost penalty compared to a system that's equally accurate but concise, and instructing a model to be appropriately brief (or asking for a structured, compact output format like a short JSON object instead of a long prose explanation) can meaningfully reduce cost without meaningfully reducing quality, in tasks where verbosity wasn't actually adding value.

sections.heading: Two Different Compute Patterns: Prefill vs. Decode
sections.body: Every LLM request runs through two phases with fundamentally different performance characteristics. The first, prefill, happens when the model reads your prompt: all of the input tokens -- whether it's 50 or 50,000 -- get pushed through the transformer's layers in a single forward pass. Each token's attention computation can be done alongside every other token's, because the full sequence is already sitting in memory before generation starts. This makes prefill embarrassingly parallel: it's dominated by large matrix multiplications that GPUs are extremely good at saturating, so throughput scales well even as prompts grow long. The second phase, decode (generation), works completely differently. The model produces exactly one output token, appends it to the sequence, then must run another full forward pass to produce the next one -- and it can't skip ahead or batch across positions within a single response, because token N+1's computation depends on having already produced token N. That structural difference, not some arbitrary business decision, is the root cause of the price gap you see in every provider's rate card.

sections.heading: Why Sequential Generation Costs More Per Token
sections.body: Decode is what's called memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. To generate a single token, the GPU has to load the entire model's weights (and the growing key-value cache of every prior token) from memory, run one comparatively tiny matrix-vector operation, then throw most of that loaded data away and reload nearly the same amount to produce the very next token. On modern hardware, moving data is slower than doing arithmetic on it, so the GPU spends most of its cycles waiting on memory transfers rather than computing -- utilization during decode commonly sits in the 10-20% range, versus 50-70%+ during prefill. Techniques like continuous batching (interleaving decode steps from many concurrent requests) claw back some of that waste, but they can't eliminate the underlying constraint: a 500-token response requires 500 sequential round-trips through the model, each one paying the same fixed memory-bandwidth tax, while a 500-token prompt pays that tax roughly once. That per-token inefficiency is what providers pass through as a several-times-higher output rate -- commonly 3x to 5x the input price, sometimes more for reasoning-heavy models.

sections.heading: Reading the Rate Cards: What the Ratio Actually Reflects
sections.body: When you compare provider pricing pages, the input/output split isn't marketing -- it's a fairly direct readout of the prefill/decode cost asymmetry described above. A frontier model might list $3 per million input tokens against $15 per million output tokens, a 5x ratio; a smaller, cheaper model might show $0.15 versus $0.60, the same 4x shape at a different scale. The ratio tends to widen further for models built around extended reasoning, where a large internal 'thinking' trace is generated token-by-token before the visible answer even starts -- all of that hidden reasoning bills as output tokens at the output rate, even though the user never reads it. This is why two requests with identical prompts and identical final answers can have wildly different bills: the one that reasoned through 2,000 internal tokens before answering pays for all 2,000 at the expensive rate, while a more direct model answering the same question might generate a fraction of that.

sections.heading: The Verbosity Tax: When Chatty Output Quietly Inflates Your Bill
sections.body: Because output tokens are the expensive side of the ledger, any habit that inflates output length -- without adding value -- becomes a direct and often invisible cost multiplier. Common offenders: a system prompt that never asks for a length constraint, so the model defaults to a few paragraphs of hedged prose where three bullet points would answer the question; a summarization task that echoes large chunks of the source text back verbatim inside the 'summary'; or a classification task where the model explains its reasoning in full sentences before finally stating the one-word label you actually needed. None of these make the answer more correct. They just mean you're paying the 3-5x output rate on tokens that a tighter prompt or format would have eliminated. At scale -- thousands or millions of requests a day -- a system that generates 400 output tokens per call versus one generating 120 tokens for equivalent quality isn't a rounding error, it's a multiple-of-the-total-bill difference.

sections.heading: Designing for Brevity: Concrete Ways to Cut Output Cost
sections.body: The fix flows directly from the mechanism: since every unnecessary output token is billed at the expensive decode rate, trimming output length without hurting quality is one of the highest-leverage cost levers available, and it costs nothing to try. Concrete tactics: explicitly instruct the model on desired length or format ('respond in one sentence,' 'return only the JSON object, no explanation'); request structured output (a compact JSON schema) instead of free-form prose whenever a downstream system will parse the answer anyway, since structured fields are almost always shorter than the equivalent explanation; and for reasoning-capable models, set or lower the reasoning-effort/thinking-budget parameter when the task doesn't actually need extended deliberation, since that hidden reasoning bills at full output price. None of this touches input cost or model choice -- it's purely about not paying for verbosity the task never needed, which is why it's often the fastest cost win available before you touch anything architectural.

quiz.question: Why is generating output tokens generally more expensive per token than processing input tokens?
options: Output tokens are billed the same as input tokens everywhere
Output generation happens sequentially, one token depending on the previous ones, making it inherently more computationally expensive per token than parallel input processing
Input tokens require more memory than output tokens
There is no cost difference between input and output tokens

quiz.question: What is a practical cost-saving implication of the input/output pricing asymmetry?
options: Always maximize output length regardless of task
Instructing a model to be appropriately concise or using a compact output format can meaningfully reduce cost without reducing quality where verbosity wasn't adding value
Input length has no bearing on cost at all
Output pricing asymmetry is irrelevant to system design

quiz.question: Why can processing input tokens happen largely in parallel while output token generation cannot?
options: Input and output are processed identically
The model can process an entire prompt's tokens together in one pass, while each generated output token depends on all previous ones
Parallel processing is only possible for output tokens
This distinction doesn't actually exist

title: Prompt Caching and Cost Savings
content: Many API calls share a large, stable prefix -- a long system prompt, a set of few-shot examples, a big block of reference material -- that's identical across many separate requests, and prompt caching lets a provider avoid reprocessing that shared prefix every single time, passing much of the savings on to you at a substantially reduced rate for the cached portion. This course covers how caching typically works in practice: the provider recognizes when a new request's beginning matches a previously-processed prompt exactly, reuses the already-computed internal representation for that matching prefix, and only pays full processing cost for the new, variable content appended after it. You'll learn the practical implication for how you structure prompts: to benefit from caching, put the stable, unchanging content first (system instructions, few-shot examples, static reference documents) and put the variable, request-specific content last (the current user question, request-specific data) -- reordering a prompt so the variable part comes first, even if the content is otherwise identical, can break the cache match and eliminate the savings entirely.

quiz.question: What does prompt caching typically require in order to produce cost savings?
options: Every request must be completely identical, including the variable parts
A stable, unchanging prefix shared across requests that the provider can recognize and reuse without reprocessing
Caching works regardless of prompt structure
Caching only applies to output tokens, never input

quiz.question: Why should stable content (like system instructions) be placed before variable content (like the user's specific question) in a prompt to benefit from caching?
options: Order has no effect on caching behavior
Caching relies on matching a prefix exactly; putting variable content first would break the prefix match and eliminate savings
Variable content should always come first for caching to work
Caching only works if there is no variable content at all

quiz.question: What is the main cost benefit of prompt caching?
options: It eliminates all API costs entirely
It substantially reduces the cost of reprocessing a shared, stable prefix across multiple requests
It only reduces latency, never cost
It doubles the cost of every request as a tradeoff for speed

title: Choosing Models for Cost Efficiency: Routing and Cascading
content: Not every request in a real application needs the most capable, most expensive model available, and this course covers model routing (also called cascading): using a cheap, fast model to handle the easy majority of requests, and escalating only the genuinely hard cases to a more expensive, more capable model. A common pattern is a lightweight classifier or the cheap model itself attempting the task first with a confidence signal -- if confidence is high, return that answer; if confidence is low or the task is flagged as complex, re-route the request to a stronger model. You'll learn how to think about the cost-quality tradeoff curve this creates: routing well can capture most of the cost savings of always using the cheap model while capturing most of the quality of always using the expensive model, but routing poorly (a bad confidence signal, or a classifier that itself costs meaningfully more than the savings it's supposed to protect) can end up costing more than just picking one model consistently. The judgment call this course builds: recognizing when the added complexity and failure modes of a routing system are worth it for the cost savings at your actual traffic volume and difficulty distribution, versus when it's premature optimization for a system that doesn't have enough scale or difficulty variance to benefit.

quiz.question: What is the core idea behind model routing or cascading for cost efficiency?
options: Always using the most expensive model for every request
Using a cheap model for easy requests and escalating only genuinely hard cases to a more expensive model
Randomly assigning models to requests with no logic
Using the cheapest model for every request regardless of difficulty

quiz.question: What can make a routing system end up costing more than just using one model consistently?
options: Routing systems always save money with no downside
A poor confidence signal or an expensive classification step can itself cost more than the savings it's meant to protect
Routing is always free to implement
This scenario is impossible in practice

quiz.question: When might model routing be premature optimization rather than a worthwhile investment?
options: When traffic volume and task difficulty variance are too low to generate meaningful savings relative to the added complexity
Routing is always worthwhile regardless of scale
Only when using open-weight models
Routing should always be implemented from day one

title: Batch Processing for Cost Reduction
content: Several major providers offer a batch or asynchronous API mode that processes requests within a longer completion window (often within 24 hours) in exchange for a substantially discounted rate, commonly around half the price of real-time synchronous calls. This course covers when this tradeoff makes sense: workloads that are not latency-sensitive, like nightly re-scoring of a large document set, bulk classification of historical records, or generating a large batch of evaluation results, are ideal candidates, since the delay costs nothing in user experience but the discount meaningfully reduces spend at scale. You'll learn the corresponding limitations: batch mode typically doesn't support streaming responses back token-by-token, isn't suitable for anything with a real-time user waiting on the other end, and often has its own submission and result-retrieval mechanics distinct from the standard real-time API, requiring separate application logic to handle. You'll leave able to correctly classify a given workload as batch-appropriate or not, based on whether a delayed result is actually acceptable for that use case, not just based on the cost savings alone.

quiz.question: What is the main tradeoff of using a batch or asynchronous API mode?
options: Higher cost in exchange for faster results
A substantially discounted rate in exchange for accepting a longer completion window and no real-time streaming
No tradeoff; batch mode is strictly better in every way
Batch mode only works with open-weight models

quiz.question: Which workload is a good candidate for batch processing?
options: A real-time customer-facing chat interface
Nightly re-scoring of a large historical document set with no user waiting on the result
A live voice assistant
Any workload requiring immediate streamed responses

quiz.question: Why is batch mode unsuitable for a real-time user-facing chat feature?
options: Batch mode is actually faster than real-time APIs
Batch mode doesn't support streaming and can take up to a completion window (often 24 hours), incompatible with a user waiting live
Real-time features cannot use LLMs at all
There is no difference between batch and real-time modes

title: Monitoring and Budgeting for LLM Spend
content: As LLM features move from prototype to production, spend can grow unpredictably and silently unless it's actively monitored, and this course covers the practices that keep it under control. Per-request cost tracking (logging token counts and computed cost alongside every call, tagged with the feature, user, or team responsible) is the foundation, since without attribution you can see total spend rising but not know which feature or which change caused it. Alerting on spend anomalies (a sudden spike well above the historical baseline, which often signals a runaway agent loop, a bug causing retries, or an unexpected traffic surge) lets you catch cost problems within hours instead of discovering them at the end of a billing cycle. You'll learn why forecasting future spend as usage scales matters for planning, not just reacting: a feature that costs $50 a day at your current 1,000 daily users may cost $5,000 a day at 100,000 users, and understanding that scaling relationship before you hit it lets you make deliberate cost-efficiency investments (caching, routing, smaller models for simple cases) ahead of time rather than in a reactive scramble once a bill arrives that's ten times larger than expected.

quiz.question: Why does per-request cost tracking need to be tagged with a feature, user, or team, rather than just tracking total spend?
options: Tagging has no practical benefit over a single total number
Without attribution, you can see total spend rising but not identify which feature or change is responsible
Total spend tracking is always sufficient on its own
Tagging is only useful for billing disputes with the provider

quiz.question: What does an unexpected spike in LLM spend, well above the historical baseline, often signal?
options: Spend spikes are always random and meaningless
A runaway agent loop, a retry bug, or an unexpected traffic surge worth investigating
Spend spikes only ever indicate normal, expected growth
This can only be caused by a pricing change from the provider

quiz.question: Why is forecasting future spend as usage scales valuable, beyond just monitoring current spend?
options: Forecasting has no practical value since costs are always linear and predictable
It reveals scaling relationships (like cost per user growing with volume) early enough to invest deliberately in cost-efficiency measures before a large unexpected bill arrives
Forecasting is only relevant to providers, not application teams
Current spend monitoring alone is always sufficient for planning

title: Agentic Systems Bootcamp: Coordinating Multiple Agents
content: A bundled sequence introducing multi-agent systems from first principles: what a multi-agent system is and when splitting work across specialist agents beats a single generalist agent, the tradeoffs between centralized orchestration and decentralized swarm coordination, and how agents actually pass state and results to one another without drowning each other in irrelevant context. Complete the linked courses in order to build a foundation before tackling failure handling and security in the advanced Multi-Agent Systems courses.

title: Context and Cost Fundamentals: Making Every Token Count
content: A bundled sequence connecting two disciplines that are really two sides of the same coin: what actually goes into a model's context window, and what that context costs you in tokens and dollars. Covers the fundamentals of context engineering, how to budget a limited context window deliberately, and how token-based pricing actually works, so you can reason about both quality and cost tradeoffs together rather than treating them as separate concerns. Complete the linked courses in order.
